title: Is it stil necessary to learn coding in depth?
author: Old_Childhood7680
selftext:
English isn’t my first language, so please excuse any 

AI coding ability is really powerful.

I am making my own little game,and im not major in computer science but i can write a little bit python, so it is quite easy to learn gdscript for me.

At first, i will coding myself for the game basic functions,until i wanna coding a shader,godot shader’s language is similar to c++,but i haven’t learned about c++, so i ask gpt to help me to make the shader.After that,im totally addicted to use codex for my program. 

But after a week has gone,the script is totally change even that i couldn’t understand it.The whole develop process like a black box it make me feel anxiety and feel uneasy.

But i still doubt myself that i won’t be as powerful as     
AI，is it necessary for me to learn coding in depth?

It makes me wonder: I know how to drive a car, but do I really need to know how the engine works?

comments.author: Sencha-Games
comments.body: You need to learn architecture. Kinda hard to learn right now without trying code yourself to see how things fail. Idk, check out design patterns.

replies.author: MysteriousCoconut31
replies.body:
Yes, and failures are the most important learning path. Deeply understand WHY something failed and what the viable alternatives are. 

Understanding architectural tradeoffs and resiliency is more important than ever.

comments.author: KoodiRonsu
comments.body: AI doesn't remove the need to actually know what you're doing. It will happily comply and build an architectural mess no-one can use to finish any project, if the project is larger than a tiny project. For that you need actual real professional level software development skills and experience which takes years to learn.

replies.author: Warsel77
replies.body: I would argue that it is the case now - is there a strong reason why in 5 years this is still the case?

replies.author: TonyZwilde
replies.body: No one can predict the future, but knowledge is never useless. Even when we code on high level languages it's still important to know how things works on the low level to make better decisions

replies.author: Warsel77
replies.body:
>but knowledge is never useless

I only half-agree to this.

If it would come for free, sure - give me all the knowledge in the world. But it does not come for free - obtaining knowledge costs time and time is limited.

People today are not becoming experts in operating a telephone switchboard because that has been replaced with more modern technology. While learning how such a switchboard works could be of some use somehow, it is likely not going to be a good bang for the buck.

replies.author: zenmatrix83
replies.body: in computer terms, your better off knowing assembly if you can more then not, do most need it these days no. do the more intense performance optimizations still use that , as far as I know. Until we get context sizes bigger then an entire project there still can and will be spots the llm gets it wrong, and starts to assume based of whats standard. You end up wasting tokens a minimum for some things you could catch if you understood properly, at worst you ship a bad product just hoping the llm is accurate.

replies.author: Warsel77
replies.body:
I look at the delta between where we were 5 years ago in this field and am trying to imagine what 5 years forward will realistically look like.

I don't see a very strong reason why good, consistent code (all based on logic and an encompassing knowledge of how each part of a thing interacts with the rest) should be out of reach based on principle.

“I can’t see any reason that anyone would want a computer of his own.” - Ken Olsen, DEC (his idea was computers would likely only be used in a timeshare model; 1970-ish)

“I predict the Internet will soon go spectacularly supernova and in 1996 catastrophically collapse.” - Robert Metcalfe, co-Inventor of the ethernet

“There’s no chance that the iPhone is going to get any significant market share. No chance.” - Steve Ballmer, CEO of Microsoft

\-- I just think we keep repeating the same: "if it isn't now it will never be" thing

replies.author: Strategic_Sage
replies.body: Keep in mind that the opposite is also true.  Many predictions of ai capabilities have turned out to be overly optimistic.  The whole issue of unknown unknowns is always a big confounder.  Advancement will be better in some areas then er expect, and worse than we expect in others.  It's not wise to assume specific outcomes without a backup plan

replies.author: 3tt07kjt
replies.body: You can get someone to explain what programming is like today, or you can come up with your own guesses about what programming is like five years from now, but I don’t think we are going to figure it out with any confidence on Reddit.

replies.author: Motor-Travel-7560
replies.body: Humans are fallible. The ai can only do what a human instructs it to do. Therefore, when the AI output doesn't match exactly what you wanted, you should be able to know how to change the code to suit your intent. Think of it like the AI giving you a house, but you want to make some modifications. You should know how to remodel a room without bringing the whole house crashing down with it.

replies.author: Warsel77
replies.body:
>The ai can only do what a human instructs it to do.

This isn't true in most ways to read this.

A python program cannot do what I didn't tell it to do.

A LLM on the other hand can very well do a lot of things I didn't tell it to do - that's the main use of it in coding. You tell it the goals you want to achieve and the constraints around it and it infers what to do from that.

I have been programming for 36 years. I have learned a lot of stuff I definitely no longer need, maybe 90% of it. I see now that for most people learning the principles of logic etc. is essential - and knowing what the influence factors to a particular outcome are - but in-depth on a particular language, I think, will become a rarer skill.

replies.author: Apprehensive_Ad_7138
replies.body: On this i totally agree...in-depth knowledge of a particular tech or language will become rare and everyone human will have to operate on some higher level of abstraction. Pretty much what happened going from machine code, low level code like assembly and high level coding with modern languages.

replies.author: Apprehensive_Ad_7138
replies.body:
There are actual measurable factors: i made a vibe coding experiment with a friend who is not a coder (he is an architect) like me; vibe coding only (so that i couldn't use my skills directly in the codebase); one simple final goal (netflix like app for streaming local files from my nas) with several bullet points for the minimum features it should have. Done with claude code.

Both the projects scored all the requisites. He implemented 3 non requested features, i implemented 12. His UI was functional but ugly, mine was more elegant. It took me 1.6b tokens, he used 8x that (because of the lack of direction in the prompt he got things that required many many reiterations on the same portion, which explains the amount of token used).  
  
This is all cause i'm a coder and ux developer, and he is not, and this alone is a huge difference in terms of money when things scale up consistently (also considering that token cost should probably increase in the future).   
  
The idea we got a "magic box" that flattens out the differences in competence is simply some kind of delusional thing in my opinion.

replies.author: Apprehensive_Ad_7138
replies.body: And it doesn't matter if the same experiment in 5 years produces a better result for him....the delta will always be there.

replies.author: Warsel77
replies.body:
This went right past the point I made. Would you like to actually address it?  
  
Because your first reply only supported what I already said ("I would argue that it is the case now") and the second bit only added two unfounded assertions.

replies.author: Apprehensive_Ad_7138
replies.body:
This is my strong reason why in 5 years the case will still be the same.   
  
Inherent difference in input quality will always create different quality in the output.  
  
Just my opinion, of course, but i think it's intrinsic in a tech that actually requires human input.

replies.author: egonosz
replies.body:
The output is as good as the input. The problem is the llms are not really capable of inventing things. You ask it for hey I want to implement an asset manager and it will implement the unreal or unity one and not because those are the best implementation, but because it was thought on unity and unreal code. 

Now you could say they just need it to teach more data, even then it would prefer the unity or unreal one.  
If you see any game ui made, by Astra you exactly know how it looks. Now this is a thing, it can be any good ai, if you do not ask it the right questions and tell it the right direction it will default to a median path, which is Russian roulette.

Giving you en example, when you write a code even in 3-5 lines of code you make tons of decisions based on your experience and based on your preference. A llm will throw out the code which matches the pattern in its context the best. 

And I now you can dump tons of docs and skills and things to try to align it, after that it will take it as a rule and it will apply unnecessary shit every where. 

If you think in five years the managers will prompt the ai, I think you are kind of misdirected, because if you want to build a software with AI that is a full time job too. (Simple tools internal tools not, production stuff yes.) 

If you think the company will hire a vibe coder when they could hire engineer, that is laughable too. 

I do not say AI cannot take the engineers job, I say the llms can’t.

replies.author: Warsel77
replies.body:
>The problem is the llms are not really capable of inventing things.

You’re stating that as a fact, but it’s empirically false under any ordinary definition of invention. LLM-based systems have already produced previously unknown mathematical constructions, algorithms, and proofs. Saying they are simply incapable of producing genuinely novel results is no longer defensible.

I can't point to a single human invention of anything that wasn't based on prior information or observation (eg data). Can you?

>I do not say AI cannot take the engineers job, I say the llms can’t.

They already did though. If that is sustainable is an entirely different question, but plenty of engineers have lost their jobs to LLMs.

comments.author: TheReviewerWildTake
comments.body:
I would recommend learning either python or C#.   
I am not sure that deep dive into shaders and c++ is necessary for beginner (maybe later if you find yourself going that route, or if you actually like c++).  
  
The most critical thing is not even that fundamental technical stuff that AI indeed knows more or less okay (with some exceptions, when it is fed old data and it sticks for some deprecated stuff etc)   
  
The critical thing which ties gamedev with coding is   
\- structural sanity of your project, clean architecture, conscious decisions on how to map of your in-game concepts with programming concepts etc.  
  
This is where AI can really produce strange mess , leaving you with no idea on how to proceed further\\change something etc.

I too  don\`t like working with projects that were made by AI. And most devs hate that too imo, because it just feels like awkward counterintuitive product (not like humans are perfect in that department, but human project is usually a lot more readable) .    
  
As for personal projects - I feel same way about black-boxes, and I love to understand what is going on, but it is also important to prioritize what you have to understand vs what can stay as a block box.  
  
For example, not knowing how your game (on code level) treats your playable characters - is very detrimental to future development.  
  
On the other hand, a piece of code that does some kind of conversion\\manipulation that acts as auxiliary lib for some niche problem - is more or less okay, and devs oftentimes have only vague understanding about libraries like this.   
As long as you understand what kind of data it expects, and what output it produces - you may leave its code for the future, for times when you will have time to dig into that etc.   


AI knows how to write syntax and how to code things that were repeated gazillion of times, but its nature makes it pretty meh for the context heavy fields.  
And gamedev IS context heavy.   
  
Only you know where are you going with your game, what are your plans, whether you want to leave a space for extra features or whether you go ultra-minimalistic, whether you gonna have feedback, whether someone will request multiplayer, whether you expect more team members, what systems compatibility you want etc. etc.   
  
Most games aren\`t that unique in terms of actual "programming tech", but they can become unique in terms of the mix of context, requirements, expectations, goals, ideas etc. That "mix" of one game will be very different from other game. AI if left on its own will just push you into whatever "average" is statistically probable for it. So learning how to pushback on architectural level - is very nice skill.

comments.author: Apprehensive_Ad_7138
comments.body:
The analogy with driving is not really matching imho...

...you need to be in control of what you are producing with code...i tried both the ends of the spectrum: coding with my skills but assisted by the AI, and delegating everything to it...the first is instructive but slow, the latter is fast but leaves you basically nothing...now i'm trying some middle ground: first the prompts are never going to be whole and generic (no "implement this system") but more like progressive instructions in a plan i decided beforehand; second, i never let code i don't understand slip by...at least at a conceptual level, i need to know where and why things happen...llm are cool cause you can just ask them to explain the code so it's even fun to review the code....when you smack into something you don't understand, study it at least on a more abstract level; third, i separate personal fun from work, so i delegate less for the gamedev and more for a production app refactor....either way, i need to have control.

That "blackbox" thing you mentioned is real and is dangerous in many context: for example, i went to the place where i work to deploy an app i refactored with claude code on a production machine (it's a factory, old stuff and such)...it didn't work and then what do you do? Without internet, without the coding agent, what do you do if you don't even know how the code works and how to read it?  
  
...but this tech is so incredibly powerful that you should embrace it and use it with a sort of personal code...you actually decide WHERE is the line of delegation: you can vibe code everything and depend completely on the tool, you can write your code and tell the llm to explain how to make it better, you can become a monster in software architecture and delegate only the code production, you can set it as interactive tutor to learn...the choice is entirely yours. Don't believe the bullshit about human worth going to zero cause WHO is behind the screen writing a prompt is what makes all the difference. 

You can see this with the tons of vibecoded projects around now...there are people who are learning stuff even with vibe coding, and people who didn't even bother to know what tools and libraries their projects used...

comments.author: CubersumGame
comments.body:
I believe it’s enough to understand the capabilities that a particular programming language provides, as well as the general nature of the tasks you’re asking an AI to solve. Having a theoretical understanding of how things work is often sufficient.

Among other things, my game uses a compact neural network: a multilayer perceptron that takes the state of a ship as input and outputs a decision on how its structure should be modified.

The model is written in C++ and packaged in the ONNX format.

I don’t know how to write C++ myself, and my knowledge of perceptrons is purely theoretical.

But that was enough for me to understand the general direction of optimization. I wanted to improve the game’s performance, I knew how that could technically be achieved and what needed to be done. So all I had to do was formulate the requirements correctly. The neural network handled the rest.

Of course, I wouldn’t have been able to review its code myself, but why would I need to if I can validate the result with extensive testing?

I don’t think this is fundamentally different from using third-party libraries from pip or NuGet. In exactly the same way, we accomplish our tasks using code written by someone else - code that we don’t review ourselves and, in some cases, wouldn’t even be able to fully understand.

comments.author: guanzo91
comments.body:
>  do I really need to know how the engine works?

You should understand it at a high level. You should be able to point at an engine part and say "This is X, it is responsible for Y, it is connected to A,B,C". 

> the script is totally change even that i couldn’t understand it

Ask AI to first do a code review. It'll suggest changes. Ask it to explain the reason behind each change, and don't stop asking it until you understand the reasoning. Do this enough and you'll slowly develop an intuition on what clean and maintainable code looks like.

comments.author: Vindelator
comments.body:
"necessary for me to learn coding in depth?"

Depends on your goals. 

Wanna work in a studio as a game dev? Yeah, you should be able to code well.

Just wanna have fun and make a game? No, you don't need to be a coder.   
  
The reality is today's AI is pretty good at coding, and it's going to be getting better every year. And if you're GOOD at using AI to make stuff, you can do a lot.

The more technology and code skills you have, the better. But time is finite.

comments.author: Odd-Bench6264
comments.body:
Modern coding agents are capable of coding games without any guidance. You don't need to learn code, you also don't need to learn "architecture" or any high level concepts.   
  
If you start building a game, the first version of the code will probably be just fine. It becomes spaghetti over time as you add stuff. And honestly - that doesn't matter that much. Coding agents can still work on it. Bugs may start appearing more often later in the development process, and that is not a deal breaker. Ask the AI to fix it. Eventually you will probably develop some intuition, like asking the agent for a general fix and not to just patch the bug.

Coding agents can also end up with a redundant code. Not at first - but over time. What can help is, if you prompt it in terms of systems.   
  
Good example: "make a system for taking damage, and account for armor, and the modifier system. Make it easy to add extra future modifiers. then apply this system on enemy y. it should take damage when hit by the sword. Future enemies should also take damage through this system".   
  
Bad example: "enemy y should take damage when hit by the sword".

Truth is, you can code a complex, well performing, bug-free game without a human ever looking at the code. If you want to be a solo game dev, coding is definately not where you should start. Focus on game design and feel, learn som basic visual skills, and leave the implementation for the coding agents.
